slides.slideTextExcerpt: A market brings buyers and sellers together. Competitive markets contain many participants, so no single buyer or seller sets the price.

textbookMatches.excerpt: A market is a group of buyers and sellers of a particular good or service. Buyers determine demand, while sellers determine supply.
textbookMatches.relationship: Both sources introduce the market as the setting where supply and demand interact. The textbook separates the two roles named together on the slide.

textbookMatches.excerpt: In a perfectly competitive market, the goods offered for sale are alike and the buyers and sellers are so numerous that each has a negligible effect on market price.
textbookMatches.relationship: This passage expands the slide’s definition of competition and explains why an individual participant cannot control price.

textbookExercises.questionExcerpt: What are the characteristics of a perfectly competitive market?

slides.slideTextExcerpt: The law of demand: when the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls, other things equal.

textbookMatches.excerpt: The quantity demanded of any good is the amount of the good that buyers are willing and able to purchase.
textbookMatches.relationship: The textbook supplies the precise definition needed to interpret the quantity axis of the demand curve shown in the lecture.

textbookMatches.excerpt: Because a lower price increases the quantity demanded, the demand curve slopes downward.
textbookMatches.relationship: This directly supports the slide’s law of demand and connects the verbal rule to the curve’s downward shape.

textbookExercises.questionExcerpt: Draw a demand curve for music downloads and show what happens when the price of a music subscription falls.
Explain whether a change in income shifts the demand curve or causes movement along it.
textbookExercises.testedKnowledgePoint: Demand shifts versus movement along the curve

slides.slideTextExcerpt: Income, related goods, tastes, expectations, and the number of buyers can shift the entire demand curve.

textbookMatches.excerpt: Any change that raises the quantity buyers wish to purchase at every price shifts the demand curve to the right and is called an increase in demand.
textbookMatches.relationship: The passage defines the rightward shift referenced by the slide and distinguishes it from a price-driven movement along the curve.

textbookExercises.questionExcerpt: List the variables that shift the demand curve and give an example of each.

slides.slideTextExcerpt: Market equilibrium occurs where the supply and demand curves intersect. At this price, quantity supplied equals quantity demanded.

textbookMatches.excerpt: At the equilibrium price, the quantity of the good that buyers are willing and able to buy exactly balances the quantity sellers are willing and able to sell.
textbookMatches.relationship: This is the textbook’s full explanation of the equality represented by the intersection on the lecture slide.

textbookMatches.excerpt: A surplus puts downward pressure on price, while a shortage puts upward pressure on price.
textbookMatches.relationship: This adds the adjustment mechanism that explains how a market moves toward the equilibrium introduced on the slide.

textbookExercises.questionExcerpt: Using a supply-and-demand diagram, identify the equilibrium price and quantity, then show the effect of a price set above equilibrium.

lectureSummary.overview: The lecture introduces how buyers and sellers interact in competitive markets, then builds from individual demand decisions to demand shifts and market equilibrium.
reviewFocus: Distinguish a change in quantity demanded from a shift in demand.
Practice identifying the variables that move the demand curve.
Use shortages and surpluses to explain movement toward equilibrium.
